target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection provides irreplaceable educational benefits and that using already-dead animals makes the practice ethically acceptable
objection: Real-animal dissection is not educationally irreplaceable because synthetic anatomical models and computer simulations can teach the same core concepts and skills without killing or dismembering animals. Also, the fact that some specimens are already dead does not solve the ethical problem, because dissection supply methods are reported to be inhumane and to harm biodiversity through wild capture.

target: AG2’s claim that models and simulations can teach the same skills and concepts as real dissection
objection: Real-animal dissection is educationally irreplaceable in practice because it gives students direct tactile contact with real tissues, exposure to natural anatomical variation, and hands-on experience with exposing and interpreting real structures; models and simulations cannot fully replicate those fine-motor, tactile, and specimen-based learning experiences.

target: AG1’s use of already-dead specimens and byproducts as a justification for dissection
objection: The claim that dissection mostly uses already-dead animals or byproducts is not enough to justify the practice, because the supply methods used to obtain dissection animals are harmful and the demand contributes to wild capture and biodiversity loss.

target: AG2’s assumption that dissection demand mainly drives inhumane wild capture and biodiversity harm
objection: If most dissection animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, then the causal link from classroom dissection demand to wild capture and biodiversity loss does not hold in the way AG2 claims.

target: AG1’s broader argument that dissection should be allowed because it is useful and uses dead animals productively
objection: Dissection is not educationally irreplaceable, because synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same core anatomy and observational skills, and the ethical defense based on already-dead animals does not address the inhumane sourcing and environmental harms associated with dissection supply chains.

target: AG2’s repeated claim that alternatives fully replace dissection’s learning value
objection: Models and simulations cannot fully replicate the tactile experience, real tissue manipulation, and variable 3D anatomical relationships of actual specimens, so they do not replace the fine-motor and observational learning that dissection provides.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is educationally valuable and that already-dead/byproduct sourcing reduces ethical concern
objection: Dissection is not educationally necessary because models and simulations can teach the same anatomy and recording skills, and the environmental problem remains because dissection demand is tied to wild capture that reduces local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection demand largely causes wild-capture harm
objection: If dissection specimens are mostly already dead and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, then the wild-capture/biodiversity-loss story AG2 relies on does not describe the relevant sourcing reality for school dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that already-dead/byproduct sourcing makes dissection ethically acceptable
objection: The fact that some specimens are already dead or are byproducts does not eliminate the broader supply-chain impact, because dissection demand still depends on wild capture and therefore still harms local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that models and simulations can teach the same anatomy and skill outcomes as dissection
objection: Real dissection uniquely requires direct manipulation of tissues, careful cutting, and learning to identify structures through texture, resistance, color, and variability, which builds fine motor skill and hand-eye coordination in ways models and simulations cannot fully match.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is necessary for core biology learning
objection: Dissection is not the only way to learn anatomy or practice observation and recording, because models and simulations can teach the same structures and relationships without killing or dismembering animals; the animal-supply chain also creates unnecessary ecological harm.

target: AG2’s claim that models and simulations can provide an adequate educational replacement for dissection
objection: Dissection gives hands-on practice with real tissues, real-time cutting decisions, and 3D anatomical relationships that models and simulations cannot fully reproduce, so the “adequate replacement” assumption is not warranted.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is useful because it teaches skills and uses dead animals productively
objection: Dissection is neither necessary nor irreplaceable for the core learning goals, and the claim that harm is minimized because animals are already dead does not address the fact that dissection supply is tied to wild capture that damages local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary because alternatives exist and that ethical concerns dominate
objection: The alternatives are too narrow in what they replicate: they do not fully provide the real-specimen, tactile, procedural learning that builds fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and understanding of natural anatomical variability, and the ethics objection rests on a sourcing assumption that does not fit the byproduct/already-dead reality.

target: AG1’s argument that dissection is worthwhile despite not being required by AP Biology, NGSS, or medical training
objection: Dissection is not required by major standards or physician training, so it is not an educational necessity, and it still imposes unacceptable ethical and environmental costs through inhumane supply methods and wild capture that reduces biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary and that alternatives can replace its benefits
objection: Dissection provides direct specimen-based learning that builds fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and science interest in ways models and simulations cannot fully replicate, and the relevant specimens are usually already dead byproducts rather than animals killed specifically for class.

target: AG1’s claim that synthetic alternatives cannot replicate dissection’s educational goals
objection: The claim that alternatives cannot replicate the educational outcomes assumes that fine motor, hand-eye coordination, and observational skills require real dead specimens, but models and simulations can be designed to train those same competencies and present anatomical variation.

target: AG2’s claim that educational alternatives and ethics concerns make dissection unnecessary
objection: Dissection uniquely offers real-specimen learning that develops procedural and sensory anatomy skills and can spark science interest, while the ethical objection is weakened if the specimens are mostly already-dead byproducts rather than animals killed for class.

target: AG1’s claim that already-dead/byproduct sourcing removes the ethical problem
objection: The relevant sourcing picture is still one of heavy wild capture, so the fact that some specimens are already dead does not remove the ecological harm created by dissection demand.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary and ethically unacceptable because of animal sourcing
objection: Even though AP/NGSS and medical training do not require dissection, it is still a valuable biology activity because it gives direct real-specimen experience and career motivation; and under the defended sourcing reality, over 98% of specimens were already deceased and fetal pigs are landfill-bound byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that already-dead/byproduct sourcing makes the wild-capture objection irrelevant
objection: The assumption that specimens are mostly already-dead byproducts is false in the relevant supply chain: approximately 99% of dissection animals are wild-caught, so wild-capture harm remains operative.

target: AG2’s claim that wild-capture harm is central to school dissection
objection: If over 98% of dissected animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, then wild-capture and biodiversity loss are not the operative harm driver in ordinary classroom dissection.

target: AG1’s response that wild-capture is not the main problem if some specimens are already dead
objection: The objection is broader than wild capture: even if some classrooms use already-dead specimens, the animal-supply chain used to provide dissection animals is still inhumane and harmful, and dissection is not educationally required because alternatives can meet the learning goals.

target: AG2’s claim that ethical and environmental harms remain despite dead/byproduct specimens
objection: If specimens are predominantly already dead and taken from byproduct channels, then dissection does not create an additional ongoing wild-capture harm stream, so the ethical/environmental rationale for opposing it does not hold in the way claimed.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct/already-dead sourcing removes the harm argument
objection: Byproduct sourcing does not eliminate the environmental harm because dissection demand still depends on a supply chain that draws animals from the wild, which contributes to declining local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection demand still drives harmful wild capture despite byproduct sourcing
objection: If most specimens are already-dead byproducts headed for disposal, then dissection demand is largely satisfied without fresh wild capture, so the specific wild-capture-to-biodiversity-loss mechanism does not apply as claimed.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct/already-dead specimens mean schools are not driving wild capture
objection: Dissection supply chains are not reliably satisfied by byproducts alone; many specimens are sourced from the wild, so dissection demand still creates incentives for ecological harm through wild-caught procurement.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection demand causes ongoing wild-capture harm in general
objection: In typical school dissection, the specimens are overwhelmingly already deceased and come from meat-industry byproduct channels, so the ongoing wild-capture and biodiversity-loss mechanism the opposition relies on does not apply in the way it claims.

target: AG1’s claim that using byproduct specimens means the upstream harm is gone
objection: Even “already dead” or “byproduct” specimens can reflect upstream animal harvesting, so purchasing them still adds demand to the supply chain; if that supply chain involves wildlife capture, dissection demand continues to create incentives that can reduce local populations and biodiversity.
